title: Hypoglycaemia in diabetes (adult)
subject: endocrinology
summary: Treat any glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L): 15 to 20 g fast-acting glucose by mouth if alert, otherwise IV 10% or 20% glucose (or IM glucagon), recheck in 10 to 15 minutes, follow with longer-acting carbohydrate, and watch for recurrence with sulfonylureas.

sections.title: Recognise and classify
items: Level 1: glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) and 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) or above. Level 2: below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L), when neuroglycopenic symptoms begin. Level 3: a severe event with altered mental or physical state needing another person's help, whatever the glucose (ADA 2026).

Adrenergic symptoms: tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger, anxiety. Neuroglycopenic: confusion, behaviour change, slurred speech, seizure, focal deficit mimicking stroke, coma. Beta-blockers and long diabetes duration blunt warning symptoms.
Check capillary glucose in every acutely unwell, drowsy, aggressive, fitting or unconscious patient with diabetes.

Main causes: insulin or sulfonylurea (glibenclamide, glimepiride, gliclazide) with missed meals, fasting, exercise, alcohol, CKD, dose errors, weight loss or interacting antibiotics. Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs alone rarely cause it.

sections.title: Conscious and able to swallow
items: Give 15 to 20 g fast-acting glucose (ADA 2026 uses 15 g): glucose tablets or gel, 150 to 200 mL fruit juice, or 3 to 4 heaped teaspoons of sugar dissolved in water. Avoid chocolate, milk or high-fat or high-protein foods for the initial treatment.
Recheck glucose after 10 to 15 minutes. If still below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), repeat, up to 3 treatments; if still low after 3 cycles or 30 to 45 minutes, give IV glucose or IM glucagon.
Once above 70 mg/dL and recovered, give 20 g of longer-acting carbohydrate (for example 2 biscuits, a slice of bread, a chapati or the next meal); double this (40 g) after glucagon.
Patients on acarbose must use pure glucose, not sugar. Automated insulin delivery (pump) users usually need only 5 to 10 g.
Do not omit the next due insulin dose, especially basal insulin in type 1 diabetes; review which dose caused the episode and adjust it.

sections.title: Unconscious, fitting, confused or nil by mouth
items: ABC, place in recovery position, nothing by mouth. Stop any IV insulin infusion.

IV glucose over about 15 minutes: 10% glucose 200 mL or 20% glucose 100 mL (20 g). If only 25% dextrose is available, 80 mL gives 20 g; give via a large vein and flush. Avoid 50% glucose where possible (extravasation injury, rebound hyperglycaemia).

No IV access: glucagon 1 mg IM (or SC), or intranasal glucagon 3 mg; keep trying for IV access. Glucagon may take 15 minutes to act and is less effective with sulfonylureas, alcohol, liver disease or starvation.
Recheck glucose after 10 minutes and repeat IV glucose if still below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). Give oral carbohydrate once awake and able to swallow.

If still nil by mouth or at risk of recurrence, continue 10% glucose at 100 mL/h and monitor glucose hourly. Restart an IV insulin infusion only after review of the dose, once glucose is above 70 mg/dL.

sections.title: Sulfonylurea-induced and prolonged hypoglycaemia
items: Sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin hypoglycaemia can recur for 24 to 36 hours after the last dose, longer in CKD and older adults: admit and monitor glucose at least hourly initially and for at least 24 to 48 hours overall.
Use a continuous 10% glucose infusion rather than repeated hypertonic boluses, which stimulate further insulin release from the beta cell.
Recurrent hypoglycaemia despite dextrose: octreotide 50 to 100 mcg SC every 6 to 8 hours (most reported adult regimen) while continuing glucose monitoring and feeding.
Stop or reduce the sulfonylurea; prefer agents with low hypoglycaemia risk. Consider deliberate overdose in unexplained or recurrent cases.

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia without a diabetes drug
items: If the patient is not on insulin or a secretagogue, consider sepsis, liver failure, renal failure, alcohol, adrenal insufficiency, drugs (quinine, co-trimoxazole, pentamidine), starvation, insulinoma or surreptitious insulin or sulfonylurea use.
Where it does not delay treatment, draw a sample at the time of hypoglycaemia for lab glucose, insulin, C-peptide, BOHB and a sulfonylurea screen, and refer to endocrinology.
After metabolic (bariatric) surgery, recurrent postprandial hypoglycaemia is recognised; refer for dietary and endocrine review (CGM can help).

sections.title: Prevent recurrence
items: Any level 2 or 3 event should prompt a review and deintensification or change of therapy (for example stop sulfonylurea, reduce basal insulin, relax the HbA1c goal in the frail).
Ask about hypoglycaemia and awareness at every visit; offer CGM to people at high risk (insulin, recurrent events, impaired awareness, CKD, cognitive impairment).
Prescribe glucagon for everyone on insulin or at high risk and teach family how to use it; ready-to-use (intranasal or prefilled) forms are preferred.

Plan for fasting (Ramadan, Navratri, other religious fasts), exercise, alcohol and illness. Clarithromycin, fluoroquinolones, co-trimoxazole, metronidazole and fluconazole potentiate sulfonylureas: reduce or pause the sulfonylurea.
Advise against driving when hypoglycaemic; check glucose before driving if on insulin or a sulfonylurea.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Discharging sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia after a single correction: recurrence is common for 24 to 36 hours.
Treating only with a glucose bolus and no follow-up carbohydrate or infusion.
Holding all insulin in type 1 diabetes after a hypo, which risks DKA.
Relying on glucagon in malnourished, alcoholic or liver disease patients (glycogen depleted).

drugs.name: Oral glucose
drugs.dose: 15 to 20 g by mouth; repeat after 10 to 15 minutes if glucose still below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), up to 3 times
drugs.notes: Then 20 g longer-acting carbohydrate. Pure glucose only if on acarbose.

drugs.name: Glucose 10% IV
drugs.dose: 200 mL (20 g) IV over 15 minutes; then 100 mL/h infusion if nil by mouth or recurrence risk
drugs.notes: Smallest effective volume in heart or renal failure.

drugs.name: Glucose 20% IV
drugs.notes: Large vein, check the cannula is patent.

drugs.name: Dextrose 25% IV
drugs.dose: 80 mL (20 g) IV slowly via a large vein, then flush
drugs.notes: Common in Indian emergency departments; hypertonic, risk of thrombophlebitis and extravasation injury.

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.dose: 1 mg IM or SC once; intranasal 3 mg; dasiglucagon 0.6 mg SC
drugs.notes: Takes up to 15 minutes. Less effective with sulfonylureas, alcohol, liver disease, starvation. Follow with 40 g carbohydrate.

drugs.name: Octreotide
drugs.dose: 50 to 100 mcg SC every 6 to 8 hours
drugs.notes: Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia recurring despite IV glucose; typical course 12 to 24 hours.
